segments.text: Taking a picture on your phone is easy.
You open the camera app, point, and tap.
For most pictures, that basic process is all you need.
But sometimes you face a specific set of conditions.
If you want a family picture and it's dark outside,
you need to turn on the flash.
Or if you're sitting high up in the stands at a hockey game
and want a picture of your favorite player,
you need to zoom in.
AI works much the same way.
Depending on the app and your subscription,
you have three specific choices you can adjust.
The model, the thinking, and the research.
You won't need to change these settings for every prompt you write,
but knowing what they do helps you get a better answer
when the context requires it.
When you use an AI app, a large language model powers its answers.
Think of the LLM as the engine inside the app.
When you choose a model, you are choosing which engine to use
based on its specific capabilities.
This graphic shows the options you have
when deciding which model to use.
The everyday model is for quick questions and simple tasks.
For example, ask, suggest a funny movie to watch tonight.
The more capable model is for more demanding tasks
with details to work through.
For example, ask, help me plan a summer business,
including costs, pricing, and how many customers I'll need.
Start with the default.
Try a more capable model when needed.
Choosing a model changes which engine you use.
The thinking setting changes how much time the AI spends
working through your task.
Think about it like a student taking an English exam.
Before they start writing the essay, they decide what to say.
Pick the examples that support their points
and organize them into an outline.
This board shows how the thinking setting manages that process.
AI isn't thinking the way a human does,
but this setting forces it to spend more time working through the task
before giving you an answer.
With less thinking, AI spends less time working through your task.
It is useful for less complicated and routine work.
For example, ask, turn these notes from our group meeting
into a clear checklist.
With more thinking, AI spends more time working through steps,
weighing options, and checking its answer.
It is useful for tasks that require analysis,
like coding, planning, and problems with steps.
For example, ask, help us divide this project among four people.
We have one week, different schedules,
and only two people know how to edit video.
Give AI more time when the task needs more working through.
There's one more option to consider.
Research.
If you stop for a fast food cheeseburger,
you already know what you want to order.
Buying your first house is a completely different process.
You have to compare prices, learn about the neighborhoods,
and check how far each house is from work before making a decision.
Regular AI chat can look simple things up for you.
Research mode handles the heavier investigations.
It gathers information from different websites
and brings it together so you can compare your options.
This chart breaks down exactly when to deploy a standard chat
versus a deep research query.
Use regular chat to get an answer to a question.
For example, ask, I live in Dallas.
How long would it take me to drive to Texas A&M in college station
versus UT Austin?
Use deep research to get information from many websites,
compare what they say, and build a report that shows sources.
For example, ask, I want to study physics
and am considering Texas A&M and UT Austin.
Compare their physics programs,
undergraduate research opportunities,
admissions requirements, and costs.
Show your sources.
Use deeper research when you need to compare information across sources.
Model, thinking, research.
Use them when the work demands more.
